{{Short description|Mathematical method}}
In mathematics, specifically in the field of [[numerical analysis]], '''Kummer's transformation of series''' is a method used to [[series acceleration|accelerate the convergence]] of an infinite series. The method was first suggested by [[Ernst Kummer]] in 1837.

== Technique ==
Let
<math display="block">A = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n</math>
be an infinite sum whose value we wish to compute, and let
<math display="block">B = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n</math>
be an infinite sum with comparable terms whose value is known.
If the limit
<math display="block">\gamma := \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n}</math>
exists, then <math>a_n-\gamma \,b_n</math> is always also a sequence going to zero and the series given by the difference, <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n - \gamma\, b_n)</math>, converges. 
If <math>\gamma \neq 0</math>, this new series differs from the original <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n</math> and, under broad conditions, converges more rapidly.<ref>Holy et al., [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26512388_On_Faster_Convergent_Infinite_Series ''On Faster Convergent Infinite Series''], Mathematica Slovaca, January 2008</ref>
We may then compute <math>A</math> as

<math display="block">A = \gamma\,B + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (a_n - \gamma\,b_n),</math>

where <math>\gamma B</math> is a constant. Where <math>a_n\neq 0</math>, the terms can be written as the product <math>(1-\gamma\,b_n/a_n)\,a_n</math>. 
If <math>a_n\neq 0</math> for all <math>n</math>, the sum is over a component-wise product of two sequences going to zero,

<math display="block">A=\gamma\,B + \sum_{n=1}^\infty (1-\gamma\,b_n/a_n)\,a_n</math>.

==Example==
Consider the [[Leibniz formula for π]]:
<math display="block">1 \,-\, \frac{1}{3} \,+\, \frac{1}{5} \,-\, \frac{1}{7} \,+\, \frac{1}{9} \,-\, \cdots \,=\, \frac{\pi}{4}.</math>
We group terms in pairs as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& 1 - \left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5}\right) -  \left(\frac{1}{7} - \frac{1}{9}\right) + \cdots \\
&\quad = 1 - 2\left(\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{63} + \cdots \right) = 1-2A
\end{align}</math>
where we identify
<math display="block">A = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{16n^2-1}.</math>
We apply Kummer's method to accelerate <math>A</math>, which will give an accelerated sum for computing <math>\pi=4-8A</math>.

Let
<math display="block">\begin{align}
B &= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{4n^2-1} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{15} + \cdots \\
&= \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{10} + \cdots
\end{align}</math>
This is a [[telescoping series]] with sum value {{frac|1|2}}.
In this case 
<math display="block">\gamma := \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{\frac{1}{16n^2-1}}{\frac{1}{4n^2-1}} = \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{4n^2-1}{16n^2-1} = \frac{1}{4} </math>
and so Kummer's transformation formula above gives 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
A &= \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left ( 1-\frac{1}{4} \frac{\frac{1}{4n^2-1}}{\frac{1}{16n^2-1}} \right ) \frac{1}{16n^2-1} \\
&= \frac{1}{8} - \frac{3}{4} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{16n^2-1}\frac{1}{4n^2-1}
\end{align}</math>
which converges much faster than the original series.

Coming back to Leibniz formula, we obtain a representation of <math>\pi</math> that separates <math>3</math> and involves a fastly converging sum over just the squared even numbers <math>(2n)^2</math>,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\pi &= 4-8A \\
&= 3 + 6\cdot\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(4(2n)^2-1)((2n)^2-1)} \\
&= 3 + \frac{2}{15} + \frac{2}{315} + \frac{6}{5005} + \cdots
\end{align}</math>
